messages.author: 5072bc7c723de57e
messages.subject: introductin to sound generation using R
parts:
i'm a musician/statistician who just discovered tuneR and seewave and would like an introduction...

i want to use it to explore the acoustics of the clarinet...can you point me to links illustrating various things people have done with tuneR?

thanks for any help!

messages.author: de80047cbc18c87e
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] introductin to sound generation using R
parts:
Dear Lee,

Thank you for your interest in seewave.

As far as I know seewave have been mainly used for bioacoustics as
testified by the papers citing the package (see
https://scholar.google.com/scholar?oi=bibs&hl=en&cites=4749102080003960435). I
have no detail information regarding tuneR.

I would be extremely happy to know that seewave can be useful for
music. Anyone from the list?

Just to mention, the help page of the function synth() has an example
for a sound roughly imitating the sound of a clarinet:

library(seewave)
clarinet <- c(1, 0, 0.5, 0, 0.14, 0, 0.5, 0, 0.12, 0, 0.17)
s <- synth(f=f, d=d, cf = 235.5, harmonics=clarinet)

I am sorry not to be able to help more,

Best regards,

Jerome

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Re: introductin to sound generation using R
parts:
This page presents an introduction to assembling music in R.
https://thomaslevine.com/!/user-2015/

The discussion is so elementary that it isn't really specific to tuneR,
but most of the examples use tuneR underneath. Unfortunately, while
source code is sometimes linked, this page kind of glosses over how you
get from a data frame to tuneR. And none of the examples use seewave.
